title: Ladybird is now in alpha
author: janvdberg
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux. I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^) Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that. If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol. Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

This actually worked amazingly well.

I tested a lot of sites.. a few that were already opened in my firefox, and a few many others.. Every single one of them rendered correctly.

This is truly amazing.. a new browser written from scratch that actually works!

The only minor issue: page scrolling is a bit jerky.. not much.. just a little bit.. it's noticeable.

A huge lots of congratulations to the Ladybird team. What a wonderful accomplishment truly this is.

children.author: simscitizen
children.textRawHtml:
Browsers are runtimes and webpages are apps. They just happen to be apps that are dynamically fetched over the network and are packaged as HTML/CSS/JS instead of as PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries.

Runtimes can have bugs or inefficiencies that cause them to use more memory than strictly necessary, but by and large most memory problems are the product of the apps (or webpages) themselves.

children.author: panta
children.textRawHtml: The view of web pages as apps and browsers as runtime environments/OSes is reasonable but in my opinion it even reinforces the idea that it should be the browser duty to contain bad behavior from web apps/pages. Browsers are well positioned to do so, as they know exactly which resources are used by each tab , and how those grow over time. Also browsers already treat web content as untrusted (sandboxing, isolation), so it would be a natural next step to extend that approach to resource usage. It would match how Operating Systems work, where it's the OS acting as an "arbiter", not the userland application.

children.author: Wowfunhappy
children.textRawHtml:
I remember when I was a Safari user, any instance of Slack I had open would get reloaded after 5 – 10 minutes with the message "this web page was reloaded because it was using two much memory", interrupting whatever I was doing.

My computer had many gigabytes of memory, so I always found this very annoying. Like, yes, Slack is a giant memory hog and that really sucks, but I can't exactly do anything about that.

Maybe Google would have the clout to actually enforce a memory limit like this, but I'm not sure whether anyone else does at this point. Apparently even Apple wasn't big enough.

children.author: YmiYugy
children.textRawHtml:
1. It would break a very large number of existing sites.
2. The vast majority of users aren’t able to make an informed decision. 
3. Browsers already have heuristics to inform users about misbehaving tabs and suspend them.
4. It hurts performance. More pressure on gc, more cache thrashing

children.author: brigandish
children.textRawHtml:
It’s all about the UI. The browser vendor could make the informed guess and say “we think this web page is using too many resources”. Certainly Google could ascertain this during its spidering. Browsers already have several similar interventions e.g. no https, script taking too long etc.

Regardless, if it improved the experience then it becomes like Firefox was in the beginning, and Chrome in the beginning, a better performing competitor about to eat market share.

children.author: throwaway2037
children.textRawHtml: I was thinking exactly the same.  Either: You have a fixed setting per page, or you get on-demand pop-ups from your browser(!) that asks if it can use more memory for this page.  It would become exhausting very quickly.  The purpose of my question was to help the original asker if this was really a good idea.  Imagine there was a fixed setting per page... and your online banking/brokerage website has a bug that causes 2x memory usage.  Suddenly, the page stops running with an error from the browser: Out of memory.  That would be so annoying.

children.author: rileymat2
children.textRawHtml:
I am not following the logic.

Say I write a static html page that loads a series of images down the page where one image will fit on your screen at any time. If the browser loads them all into memory at once without releasing the memory or maintains the a fully rendered virtual page out of sight, is that bloat the app or runtime fault?
